```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "yu2021")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/08_yu2021_spectral_mait.R first. ",
      "See the section 'Reproducing this'."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}

measures <- ReadOutput("sample_measures.csv")
verdicts <- ReadOutput("claim_verdicts.csv")
```

## Why this dataset

A conventional analyser assigns one detector to one fluorochrome. A spectral
analyser records the emission of every fluorochrome across 64 detectors and
then solves for the contribution of each one, which is why a spectral panel
carries 35 markers where a conventional panel carries 20.

This report uses FlowRepository FR-FCM-Z3WR, the flow cytometry deposit of Yu
and colleagues [1]. The paper reports that circulating mucosal-associated
invariant T cells fall in COVID-19, and that the fall is larger in females. The
files come from a Cytek Aurora, the panel carries 35 named markers, and the
deposit holds 83 samples from 45 subjects.

The dataset was chosen because the claim can be tested. The paper states ten
findings that rest on the flow data alone, and Table S1 of the paper carries the
sex, the severity rank, the time point and the seroconversion status of every
sample. The claims live in `gating/yu2021_paper_claims.csv` with the sentence
each one came from, so a reader can check the claim against the paper before the
number is checked against the data.

```{r}
#| label: panel

panel <- ReadOutput("panel.csv")
named <- panel[panel$is_marker == TRUE, ]
kable(
  data.frame(
    Measure = c("Parameters in the file", "Named markers",
                "Unnamed fluorescence channels", "Scatter and time channels",
                "Samples", "Subjects", "Median events per sample"),
    Value = c(
      nrow(panel), nrow(named),
      sum(!panel$is_marker & !grepl("^(FSC|SSC|Time)", panel$channel)),
      sum(grepl("^(FSC|SSC|Time)", panel$channel)),
      nrow(measures), length(unique(measures$alias_subject_id)),
      format(median(measures$total_events), big.mark = ",")
    )
  ),
  caption = "The deposit. The instrument is a four laser Cytek Aurora running SpectroFlo 2.2.0.2."
)
```

The panel carries 35 named markers and one unnamed channel, which is the
viability dye. That makes 36 fluorescence parameters, and the paper describes
itself as 36 colour flow cytometry. The file and the sentence agree.

```{r}
#| label: markers

kable(
  data.frame(Marker = paste(named$marker, collapse = ", ")),
  caption = "Every named marker in the panel."
)
```

## Methods

### The dataset

FlowRepository FR-FCM-Z3WR holds 83 FCS files from 45 subjects acquired on a
four laser Cytek Aurora running SpectroFlo 2.2.0.2. The panel carries 35 named
markers and one unnamed viability channel, for 36 fluorescence parameters.
Samples were collected across 12 acquisition dates between 29 May 2020 and 16
September 2020. Metadata for sex, severity rank, time point and seroconversion
status was derived from Table S1 of the paper and joined on the subject code
that the file name uses.

### Preprocessing

The files were exported from SpectroFlo after unmixing, so they carry one column
per fluorochrome and no spillover matrix. The keyword `APPLY COMPENSATION` reads
`FALSE` in all 83 files. Compensation was not applied. The viability channel
does not carry a marker name, so the function that selects fluorescence channels
by the `$PnS` keyword was replaced by one that keeps every channel that is not
scatter and not time. The transform was applied to all 36 fluorescence
parameters.

### Gating

An openCyto template was used for sequential gating. Cut points were fitted once
on a pooled subsample of all 83 files, and the same cut was applied to every
sample. Marker cuts were placed at a minimum of the pooled density where one
existed. The CD45RA cut was set from the CD4 T cell density, because the CD8
gate density has no minimum in the positive region.

### Statistics

The Mann-Whitney test was used for two group comparisons and the Spearman
correlation for associations, matching the tests the paper itself used. Each of
the ten claims from the paper was tested against the deposited files. For claims
about time windows, significance at p below 0.05 was the criterion, matching the
paper's figure legends. A CD45RA sensitivity sweep was run at every cut from 2.4
to 4.2. FlowSOM clustering was run with 15 metaclusters on all live CD45
positive events and with 10 metaclusters inside the CD8 gate.

### Software

The analysis used flowCore, openCyto, FlowSOM and ggplot2. Every package version
is pinned in the container and asserted at build time.

## Part 1: what spectral changes about the pipeline

Compensation is not required and the viability channel requires a different
selection function. The cohort requires a single set of cut points across all
samples.

## Part 2: the cohort, and where the grouping comes from

```{r}
#| label: cohort

design <- ReadOutput("cohort_design.csv")
kable(
  design,
  caption = "The cohort. Sampling was sex balanced by design, and a subject can appear at several time points.",
  col.names = c("Severity rank", "Sex", "Samples", "Subjects")
)
```

All 83 files match a metadata row, and the metadata marks exactly 83 samples as
included in the flow analysis, so the join is complete in both directions. The
83 samples collapse to 45 subjects, with one subject contributing up to five
samples. Every test treats a sample as independent. That treatment inflates the
apparent precision, and the discussion returns to it.

## Part 3: one cut for the cohort, and the marker where that fails

Cut points were fitted once on a pooled subsample and applied to every sample.

```{r}
#| label: cuts

cuts <- ReadOutput("gate_cuts.csv")
kable(
  cuts[, c("marker", "parent", "side", "cut", "source")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Every cut point, on the logicle scale. The file gating/yu2021_gate_cuts.csv holds the reason for each one.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "Parent", "Keep", "Cut", "Source")
)
```

Six of the seven marker cuts sit on a real minimum of the pooled density. CD3
has a minimum at 3.32, CD8 at 3.29, CCR7 at 3.23 and CD161 at 3.37, and each of
them sits between two clear peaks. CD45RA has no such minimum inside the CD8
gate. The only minima of its density are at 0.08 and 0.74, which sit in the far
negative tail where almost no events are. A gate placed there calls 94 percent
of CD8 T cells positive, and the central memory and effector memory gates hold
no events at all.

The same reagent does resolve on CD4 T cells, where the density has a minimum at
2.54, and that value is used for CD8 T cells as well. The cut is recorded as a
choice in the source column of the cuts table. Part 5 measures what the choice
changes.

```{r}
#| label: hierarchy

kable(
  ReadOutput("gating_hierarchy.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The hierarchy, as the median across the 83 samples.",
  col.names = c("Step", "Median", "Unit")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: failures

failures <- ReadOutput("gating_failures.csv")
cat(sprintf(
  "%d of %d files were gated. %d failed.\n",
  nrow(measures), nrow(measures) + nrow(failures), nrow(failures)
))
```

Two numbers say that the gates are in a sensible place. CD8 T cells are 32
percent of CD3 positive cells, which is the expected fraction in blood, and
CD161hi cells are 9.1 percent of CD8 T cells, which is the range that the
literature reports for MAIT cells. One number says that a gate is not in a
sensible place. NK cells are 16.5 percent of CD45 positive cells, which is about
half of the CD3 negative parent, and B cells, monocytes and dendritic cells also
live there. The CD56 cut at 2.12 is too permissive.

That gate feeds claim 10 alone, which asks only whether NK cells carry more CD56
than CD8 T cells, and a permissive gate makes that comparison harder rather than
easier. No other number in this report depends on it.

### What CD161hi is, and is not

The panel carries no Va7.2, so it cannot identify a MAIT cell by the invariant T
cell receptor. The paper reads MAIT cells as CD8 positive CD161hi T cells, and
it validates that surrogate with single cell RNA sequencing, where the CD161hi
cluster co-expresses `KLRB1`, `CD3D`, `CD8A` and `TRAV1-2`. This report tests
the flow claims only. It inherits the surrogate and does not check it.

## Part 4: the paper's claims against its own data

```{r}
#| label: group-medians

kable(
  ReadOutput("group_medians.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "CD161hi, memory and naive frequencies, as the median of each group.",
  col.names = c("Severity rank", "Sex", "Samples", "CD161hi percent",
                "Memory percent", "Naive percent")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: claims

kable(
  verdicts[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "figure", "detail", "observed",
               "p_value", "verdict")],
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Every claim the paper makes from the flow data, tested against the deposited files.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "What the paper says", "Figure", "Measured",
                "Direction found", "p", "Verdict")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: verdict-counts

kable(
  as.data.frame(table(verdicts$verdict)),
  caption = "How the ten claims came out.",
  col.names = c("Verdict", "Claims")
)
```

Eight of the ten claims reproduce and two are partly reproduced. The two partial
ones are claims 5 and 6, which are the only claims about time points, and the
next section is about them.

The p value is the test the paper itself used, Mann-Whitney for a two group
comparison and Spearman for a correlation. A direction can be right while the
test is not significant, and claims 2, 4 and 7 are exactly that. Claim 9 also
sits above 0.05, and there the absence of a difference is the claim itself.
Eight of the ten claims are directional, so their verdict compares the direction
found against the direction stated. Claims 5 and 6 are not directional, and the
first version of this analysis treated them as directional before the criterion
was corrected.

### The headline claim

```{r}
#| label: severity-figure
#| fig-cap: "CD161hi cells against severity rank, with the Mann-Whitney p between the sexes within each rank. The paper's Figure 1G and Figure 2B are the same comparison."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd161hi_by_severity.png"))
```

CD161hi cells fall as severity rises, with a Spearman rho of -0.236 and a p of
0.031 across 83 samples. That is the title of the paper's Figure 1. The sex
difference is larger than the severity difference. Healthy females carry a
median of 30.1 percent CD161hi cells among CD8 T cells and healthy males carry
6.3 percent. By the hospitalized group the two values are 2.5 and 3.3 percent.

```{r}
#| label: slope-figure
#| fig-cap: "The regression of Figure 2C. The female slope is -5.07 percentage points per severity rank and the male slope is -1.31."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd161hi_slope_by_sex.png"))
```

The female slope is about four times the male slope. The paper writes that
females had a more dramatic loss of peripheral CD161hi cells compared with
males, and the deposited data says the same thing.

### The two claims about time points, and a mistake this report made

Claim 5 states that the greater abundance of CD161hi cells in females was lost
at early and middle time points but not in late disease. The first version of
this analysis tested that claim by asking which sex was numerically higher in
each window. Females came out higher in all three windows, so the claim was
reported as failing.

That test was wrong, and the paper says so in the legend of its Figure 2, which
states that significance was determined by a Mann-Whitney test and that an
asterisk means p below 0.05. A difference that is lost is one that stops being
significant. It keeps a direction while it is lost. A question about which sex
is higher answers a question the paper never asked, and it reports a failure
whenever an effect shrinks without a reversal, which is the normal way an effect
disappears. The test now compares the significance pattern instead.

```{r}
#| label: timepoint-figure
#| fig-cap: "CD161hi cells by time after symptom onset, with the Mann-Whitney p between the sexes in each window. This is the comparison of Figure 2E."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd161hi_by_timepoint.png"))
```

Two of the three windows match the paper exactly. The difference is not
significant at early, with a p of 0.625, and not significant at middle, with a p
of 0.824, which is what the paper means by lost. At late the paper found a
significant difference and this analysis finds a p of 0.065, which misses the
threshold by 0.015. Claim 5 is therefore partly reproduced, and the part that
fails is one window that lands just outside significance rather than a pattern
that runs the wrong way.

```{r}
#| label: memory-figure
#| fig-cap: "CD8 memory cells by time after symptom onset. Claim 6 expects a significant difference in all three windows."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("memory_by_timepoint.png"))
```

Claim 6 is the same shape of statement about the memory compartment, and it
comes out the same way once it is tested on the same criterion. Males sit above
females in every window. The difference is significant at early, with a p of
0.025, and at late, with a p of 0.009, and it is not significant at middle, with
a p of 0.198. Both time point claims therefore land two windows out of three,
and each one misses a different window. Neither miss is a reversal.

### Whether the miss is ours

Three explanations were tested before the claims were reported as partial. The
first is the inclusion rule. The paper's Figure 2E is about time after symptom
onset, which only an infected person has, and the time windows in Table S1 also
carry 18 samples from exposed contacts who were never infected. The late window
is 11 exposed against 13 infected. A test restricted to the 53 confirmed
COVID-19 samples does not rescue either claim. It weakens every window, because
it removes a third of the samples, and the late p for claim 5 moves from 0.065
to 0.225.

The second explanation is the repeated sampling. One value per subject per
window, so that nobody counts more than once, leaves both claims where they are.
The late p for claim 5 moves from 0.065 to 0.073.

The third is the time window definition. The paper sets early at 14 days or
less, middle at 15 to 21 days and late at over 21 days. The `timepoint` column
of Table S1 matches that rule on every one of the 68 samples that carries a day
count, with no sample on the wrong side of a boundary. The windows are the
authors' own.

None of the three changes the answer, so the remaining gap is between a p of
0.065 in 24 samples and a p below 0.05 in the authors' own analysis.

## Part 5: what the CD45RA choice changes

Three of the ten claims are about the memory compartment, and the memory
compartment rests on the CD45RA cut, which Part 3 established is a choice rather
than a fit. The analysis therefore runs again at every cut from 2.4 to 4.2.

```{r}
#| label: sweep

kable(
  ReadOutput("cd45ra_sweep.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The three memory claims at every CD45RA cut. The file is read once and every cut is answered from the same events.",
  col.names = c("CD45RA cut", "Memory percent, median", "Naive percent, median",
                "Claim 4", "Claim 6", "Claim 8")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: sweep-figure
#| fig-cap: "The same table as a figure. No verdict changes anywhere in the range."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cd45ra_sweep.png"))
```

The memory frequency moves from 55.5 to 65.3 percent across the range. No
verdict changes. The cut point is not measurable from the data, and it does not
matter, because all three claims are comparisons between two groups gated at the
same place. A cut that is wrong by the same amount in both groups cancels.

## Part 6: clustering as a second route

Sequential gating asks how many cells fall inside a boundary. Clustering asks
how many groups are in the data. The second question needs no hierarchy, so it
is a genuine second route to the same population.

```{r}
#| label: umap
#| fig-cap: "FlowSOM metaclusters on 249,000 live CD45+ events, drawn 3,000 per sample, which is the draw the paper used for its Figure 1B."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_metaclusters.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-markers
#| fig-cap: "The same embedding, coloured by each lineage marker."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_markers.png"))
```

### Fifteen metaclusters on all leucocytes cannot find MAIT cells

The first attempt clustered every live CD45 positive event into 15 metaclusters
and looked for the CD161 high cluster among the CD8 T cell clusters. It selected
a metacluster of 484 events whose brightest marker was CD56, at a median of
4.41, and whose CD161 median of 2.66 ranked fifth of the fifteen clusters. That
is an NK cell cluster, not a MAIT cluster.

The reason is the size of the population. CD161hi cells are 9 percent of CD8 T
cells, which is under 2 percent of the CD45 positive parent, and a rare
population is absorbed by a neighbouring metacluster when the number of
metaclusters is fixed in advance.

### Clustering inside the CD8 gate does find them

```{r}
#| label: cd8-clusters

kable(
  ReadOutput("cd8_cluster_median_expression.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Ten metaclusters fitted inside the CD8 gate on 56,124 pooled events. Metacluster 9 carries a CD161 median of 3.76 against 2.46 in the runner up."
)
```

The MAIT metacluster is chosen by the highest median CD161, and no cluster is
named by eye.

```{r}
#| label: route-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Every sample, gated and clustered. The dashed line is equality."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("route_comparison.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: clustering-claims

kable(
  ReadOutput("claim_verdicts_clustering.csv")[
    , c("claim_id", "short_name", "detail", "observed", "p_value", "verdict")
  ],
  digits = 4,
  caption = "The five CD161hi claims again, read from the metacluster instead of the gate.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "What the paper says", "Measured", "Direction found",
                "p", "Verdict")
)
```

The metacluster holds 9.14 percent of the pooled CD8 gate and the gate holds a
median of 9.13 percent. The two routes agree at a Spearman rho of 0.959 across
the 83 samples, and they reached that number by different means. One route
fitted a boundary on one marker. The other grouped events in eight dimensions
and never saw a gate.

All five claims come out the same way by both routes. Four reproduce and claim 5
is partly reproduced, and it misses on the same window for the same reason. The
clustering route gives the late window a p of 0.065, which is the value the
gating route gives it to three decimal places. The late window misses
significance under a boundary fitted on one marker and under a metacluster
fitted in eight dimensions, so the miss is a property of these 24 samples and
not of the gate.

## Discussion

### What this shows

A published finding from a 35 marker spectral panel reproduces from the
deposited files, with an analysis that shares no code and no software with the
original. The authors used FlowJo and Omiq. This analysis used flowCore, FlowSOM
and one CSV of cut points. Eight of ten claims come out as the paper states
them, and the central one comes out by two independent routes that agree at rho
0.959.

The two partial claims are the two about time points, and each lands two windows
out of three. Neither miss is a reversal. Claim 5 needs a significant difference
at late and finds p 0.065, and claim 6 needs one at middle and finds p 0.198.

### The failure that was ours

The first version of this report said that claim 5 did not reproduce, because
females were numerically higher in all three windows. That was a mistake in the
test, not a finding about the data. The paper states its criterion in the legend
of its Figure 2, which is a Mann-Whitney test with an asterisk at p below 0.05,
and a difference that is lost is one that stops being significant rather than
one that reverses.

The lesson generalises past this dataset. A claim of the form "the difference
disappeared" is a claim about detectability. A claim about direction guarantees
a false failure, because an effect that shrinks to nothing still points
somewhere. The claims file now records the criterion for each claim next to the
sentence it came from, so the encoding is reviewable rather than buried in the
test.

### Where the fragility sits

A gate on a bimodal marker is a fit and a gate on a continuum is a decision.
This dataset separates the two cases inside one panel. CD3, CD8, CCR7 and
CD161 are bimodal, their cuts were fitted from the pooled density, and the
analysis inherits nothing from the analyst at those four gates. CD45RA is a
continuum, its cut cannot be fitted, and the analysis inherits a number that a
person chose. The sweep in Part 5 then shows that the chosen number changes the
frequency by ten percentage points and changes no conclusion.

A cut point matters when the reported quantity is a frequency. It cancels when
the reported quantity is a comparison between two groups gated at the same
place.

### What this does not show

It does not show that the paper is right. It shows that the numbers in the paper
follow from the files the authors deposited, and a shared error in the panel, in
the staining or in the cohort would survive this check untouched. Nor does it
test the MAIT surrogate. Every number here is CD161hi within CD8 T cells,
because the panel has no Va7.2, and whether that population is MAIT cells rests
on the sequencing in the paper.

The 83 samples come from 45 subjects, and every test treats a sample as
independent. A subject who contributes five samples counts five times. That
treatment inflates the precision of every p value in Part 4, and it affects the
claims about time points most, because those windows are built from repeated
sampling of the same people. A mixed model with a subject random effect is the
correct test, and it is not run here.

The normal group holds five females and five males. The largest effect in the
report, a median of 30.1 percent against 6.3 percent, rests on those ten
samples. The direction is clear and ten people do not settle the magnitude.

### What is left to do

The dataset carries 12 acquisition dates between 29 May 2020 and 16 September
2020, and no batch correction was applied. CytoNorm is the tool for that, and it
is not in the container, because it is on GitHub only and not on Bioconductor.
CytoNorm would test whether the severity correlation survives batch correction,
and that is the next check this analysis needs.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull this dataset only, not the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/FlowRepository_FR-FCM-Z3WR_files

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/08_yu2021_spectral_mait.R

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/yu2021_spectral_mait.qmd
```

The clinical grouping comes from Table S1 of the paper. It is derived into
`gating/yu2021_sample_metadata.csv`, which is committed, so the join does not
depend on a download.

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
